# Introduction

Every likelihood in this course so far has assumed that observed case counts
follow a Poisson distribution:

$$\text{obs}_t \sim \text{Poisson}(\rho \cdot I_t)$$

That is a modelling choice, and it makes a specific claim about how observation
works. This session asks whether the claim holds, what happens when it does not,
and what a likelihood is really doing when you fit with one.

# Objectives

In this session you will:

1. Critically evaluate observation model choices (Poisson, negative binomial)
2. Check whether the Poisson variance assumption holds for real data
3. Understand negative log-likelihood as an implicit distance metric
4. Make informed choices about observation models for your own research

# Load Tristan da Cunha data

We'll use the same influenza outbreak data from 1971:

```{julia}
# Load data
flu_tdc = CSV.read(datadir("flu_tdc_1971.csv"), DataFrame)

# Plot
scatter(
    flu_tdc.time, flu_tdc.obs,
    xlabel = "Time (days)", ylabel = "Daily incidence",
    label = "Observed cases", markersize = 4, color = :red,
    title = "Tristan da Cunha 1971 Influenza Outbreak",
    legend = :topright
)
```

We have `{julia} length(flu_tdc.time)` daily observations of case counts.

# Simple SIR model for comparison

For this session, let's use a simpler SIR model to make the concepts clearer:

```{julia}
"""
Simple SIR model for pedagogical purposes.
"""
function simulate_sir(θ, init_state, times)
    R_0, D_inf = θ[:R_0], θ[:D_inf]

    function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
        S, I, R = u
        β, γ = p
        N = S + I + R

        du[1] = -β * S * I / N
        du[2] = β * S * I / N - γ * I
        du[3] = γ * I
    end

    β = R_0 / D_inf
    γ = 1.0 / D_inf
    u0 = [init_state[:S], init_state[:I], init_state[:R]]
    prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, (times[1], times[end]), [β, γ])
    sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(), saveat=times)

    # Extract incidence (new infections per day)
    S_values = sol[1, :]
    incidence = [0.0; -diff(S_values)]

    return DataFrame(time=times, S=S_values,
                     I=sol[2, :],
                     R=sol[3, :],
                     Inc=incidence)
end
```

```{julia}
# Try some parameters
times = flu_tdc.time
θ_test = Dict(:R_0 => 10.0, :D_inf => 2.5)
init_test = Dict(:S => 270.0, :I => 3.0, :R => 0.0)

traj_test = simulate_sir(θ_test, init_test, times)

# Plot
plot(traj_test.time, traj_test.Inc,
     label="Predicted incidence", linewidth=2, color=:blue)
scatter!(flu_tdc.time, flu_tdc.obs,
         label="Observed cases", markersize=4, color=:red,
         xlabel="Time (days)", ylabel="Cases",
         title="SIR Model vs Observed Data")
```

Not a perfect fit, but good enough for illustration!

In your own work, you should run [prior and posterior predictive checks](model_checking.qmd) when fitting models. We skip them here to focus on observation model choices.
# Approach 1: Poisson Likelihood (Traditional)

## The standard approach

This is what we've been doing throughout the course:

```{julia}
@model function sir_poisson(times, init_state, n_obs)
    # Priors
    R_0 ~ Uniform(1.0, 20.0)
    D_inf ~ Uniform(1.0, 10.0)
    ρ ~ Uniform(0.1, 1.0)  # Reporting rate

    # Simulate
    θ = Dict(:R_0 => R_0, :D_inf => D_inf)
    traj = simulate_sir(θ, init_state, times)

    # Likelihood: Poisson observation model
    lambdas = [max(ρ * traj.Inc[i], 1e-10) for i in 1:n_obs]
    obs ~ arraydist(Poisson.(lambdas))

    return traj
end
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reminder: `arraydist` and `|` conditioning
`obs ~ arraydist(Poisson.(lambdas))` declares a vector of independent Poisson observations, one per time point. The `|` operator, applied when creating the model instance below, conditions the model on the actual data. See the [MCMC session](mcmc.qmd) for a full explanation of this pattern.
:::

We fit this model:

```{julia}
# Fit with NUTS
model_poisson = sir_poisson(times, init_test, length(flu_tdc.obs)) | (; obs = flu_tdc.obs)
chain_poisson = sample(model_poisson, NUTS(0.65), 500, progress=false)
# The 0.65 is the target acceptance rate for NUTS — higher values (closer to 1)
# make the sampler more conservative, lower values allow larger steps.
# The default 0.65 works well for most models.
```

```{julia}
# Plot posteriors
plot(chain_poisson[[:R_0, :D_inf, :ρ]], size=(900, 600))
```

```{julia}
# Summary statistics
summarystats(chain_poisson)
```

## What does Poisson assume?

The Poisson distribution has a key property: **variance = mean**

```{julia}
# Illustrate Poisson assumption
λ_values = [5, 20, 50]
p = plot(title="Poisson Distribution: Variance = Mean",
         xlabel="Count", ylabel="Probability")

for λ in λ_values
    dist = Poisson(λ)
    x_range = max(0, λ-20):min(λ+20, λ*2)
    plot!(p, x_range, [pdf(dist, x) for x in x_range],
          label="λ=$λ (σ²=$λ)", linewidth=2)
end
p
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: Does the assumption hold for our data?"}
The Poisson model claims the variance of the observations equals their mean. Check
whether that is plausible for the Tristan da Cunha data.

1. Fit the Poisson model above and extract the posterior mean trajectory.
2. Compute the residuals (observed minus predicted) and their variance.
3. Compare that variance against the mean prediction. If the data were Poisson,
   the two should be roughly equal.

What do you find, and what would it imply for the parameter estimates?
:::

```{julia}
# Residual variance against mean prediction, under the Poisson fit
θ_fit = Dict(:R_0 => mean(chain_poisson[:R_0]), :D_inf => mean(chain_poisson[:D_inf]))
pred_fit = mean(chain_poisson[:ρ]) .* simulate_sir(θ_fit, init_test, times).Inc
resid_fit = flu_tdc.obs .- pred_fit

println("mean prediction:    ", round(mean(pred_fit), digits = 2))
println("residual variance:  ", round(var(resid_fit), digits = 1))
println("ratio:              ", round(var(resid_fit) / mean(pred_fit), digits = 1),
        "  (Poisson demands 1)")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
The ratio printed above is around 25, where Poisson demands 1. The data are wildly
*overdispersed* relative to Poisson.

Two things produce that, and it is worth keeping them apart. Some of it is
genuine observation noise: two islanders infected in the same household are not
independent draws, and reporting was not uniform across the outbreak. Most of it
here is something else, namely that a single-wave SIR fitted to a two-wave
outbreak is wrong about the mean, and everything it gets wrong about the mean
lands in the residuals.

Either way the consequence for the Poisson fit is the same.
It treats every departure from the trajectory as strong evidence against it, so the posterior comes out far too narrow.
Nor can it buy its way out by moving the parameters: the four days around the observed peak are underpredicted roughly tenfold and stay that way, because the many low-count days of the second wave outweigh them.
The negative binomial in the next section loosens that grip, but notice that it does so by explaining the misfit as noise rather than by fixing the model.
:::

Reasons the assumption might fail for epidemic data:

- Under-reporting might be systematic rather than random
- Behavioural changes might create clustering
- Surveillance quality might vary over time

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: Predict what the negative binomial will change"}
Before you fit it, commit to an answer for each of these. Write them down — the
point is to be caught out if you are wrong.

1. Will the posterior for $R_0$ get **wider**, **narrower**, or stay about the
   same?
2. Will the posterior **mean** of $R_0$ move much?
3. The model adds one parameter, $\phi$. If the data were genuinely Poisson,
   what value would you expect the posterior for $\phi$ to favour?

Then fit it below and check.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
1. **Wider**, and by a lot. The negative binomial can attribute a departure from
   the trajectory to observation noise, so the data pin the parameters down less
   tightly. Here the posterior standard deviation for $R_0$ grows roughly
   fourfold. Loosening the observation model transfers uncertainty back to the
   parameters, which is the honest direction: the Poisson intervals were narrow
   because the model was forbidden from admitting the data were noisy.

2. **The mean moves too, and that is the surprise.** $R_0$ goes from about 1.8
   to about 2.6, several Poisson standard deviations apart. The two models do not
   merely disagree about the uncertainty, they disagree about the answer.

   The shortfall sits almost entirely in the first wave.
   Days 6 to 9 carry about four fifths of the squared residual, and day 7 alone about a third: 47 cases reported against fewer than five predicted.
   The fitted trajectory accounts for about 192 of the 312 reported cases, and nearly all of the gap is there.
   The Poisson fit cannot lift its peak to meet those days, because the outbreak has a second wave and a single SIR curve has only one peak to spend.
   Days 19 to 59 carry 109 of the 312 cases and rise again to 12 on day 32.
   Raising $R_0$ makes the epidemic burn out sooner: at $R_0 = 7$, holding $D_\mathrm{inf}$ at its fitted value, the trajectory peaks on day 4 and predicts almost no cases at all after day 19, where the Poisson likelihood then gives those 109 observed cases essentially no probability.
   Fitting the same model to the first eighteen days alone removes the second wave, and $R_0$ comes out around 7.

   The negative binomial adds a dispersion parameter, so departures from its mean cost much less: over days 19 to 59 its log-likelihood is about 40 units better than the Poisson's.
   Less bound to track every day exactly, it settles on a longer infectious period and a larger $R_0$, and so on a larger predicted total, about 233 cases against 192.

   Look at $\rho$ in the comparison table below. The Poisson fit pushes it to about
   0.99, against the upper bound of its `Uniform(0.1, 1.0)` prior. A parameter
   pinned to the edge of its prior is a model straining against a constraint, and
   here it is straining for the same reason: reporting everybody is the only other
   way to make the totals add up.

3. **Large $\phi$** is the right answer to the question as asked, because
   variance is $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$ and the second term vanishes as
   $\phi \to \infty$. What the data actually say is the opposite: the posterior
   for $\phi$ sits near 0.5, so the variance is roughly $\mu + 2\mu^2$ and the
   extra flexibility was very much needed.

   Note that a small $\phi$ is not proof of messy reporting. A single-wave SIR
   cannot reproduce a two-wave outbreak, and the negative binomial is absorbing
   that structural failure as though it were noise. An observation model will
   always volunteer to explain a misspecified mean, which is why the
   [model checking](model_checking.qmd) session comes first.
:::

# Approach 2: Negative Binomial Likelihood (Pragmatic)

## Adding overdispersion

When Poisson doesn't fit well (variance > mean), we often use Negative Binomial:

$$\text{obs}_t \sim \text{NegativeBinomial}(\mu_t, \phi)$$

where:

- $\mu_t = \rho \cdot I_t$ (mean)
- $\phi$ controls overdispersion (variance = $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$)

```{julia}
@model function sir_negbin(times, init_state, n_obs)
    # Priors
    R_0 ~ Uniform(1.0, 20.0)
    D_inf ~ Uniform(1.0, 10.0)
    ρ ~ Uniform(0.1, 1.0)
    φ ~ Exponential(10.0)  # Overdispersion parameter

    # Simulate
    θ = Dict(:R_0 => R_0, :D_inf => D_inf)
    traj = simulate_sir(θ, init_state, times)

    # Likelihood: Negative Binomial observation model
    mus = [max(ρ * traj.Inc[i], 1e-10) for i in 1:n_obs]
    # NegativeBinomial(r, p) where r=φ, p=φ/(φ+μ)
    obs ~ arraydist([NegativeBinomial(φ, φ/(φ+μ)) for μ in mus])

    return traj
end
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Code explainer
- [`NegativeBinomial(r, p)`](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/univariate/#Distributions.NegativeBinomial) - Julia's parameterisation uses `r` (number of successes) and `p` (success probability). To get mean `μ` with overdispersion `φ`, use `r=φ` and `p=φ/(φ+μ)`. This gives variance = `μ + μ²/φ`, so larger `φ` approaches Poisson, smaller `φ` gives more overdispersion.
:::

Now fit it, so that the predictions you just committed to can be checked.

```{julia}
model_negbin = sir_negbin(times, init_test, length(flu_tdc.obs)) | (; obs = flu_tdc.obs)
chain_negbin = sample(model_negbin, NUTS(0.65), 500, progress=false)
summarystats(chain_negbin)
```

```{julia}
# Compare the two observation models on the parameter they disagree about most
comparison = DataFrame(
    parameter = ["R_0", "D_inf", "ρ"],
    poisson_mean = [mean(chain_poisson[p]) for p in (:R_0, :D_inf, :ρ)],
    poisson_sd = [std(chain_poisson[p]) for p in (:R_0, :D_inf, :ρ)],
    negbin_mean = [mean(chain_negbin[p]) for p in (:R_0, :D_inf, :ρ)],
    negbin_sd = [std(chain_negbin[p]) for p in (:R_0, :D_inf, :ρ)],
)
comparison.sd_ratio = round.(comparison.negbin_sd ./ comparison.poisson_sd, digits = 1)
comparison
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check the chain before trusting the comparison

Both fits here are 500 NUTS draws, which is enough to see the difference in
question but not enough to report. The negative binomial chain in particular comes
back with a tail effective sample size in the tens for $\rho$, so treat the third
decimal of anything above as noise. The [diagnostics session](mcmc_diagnostics.qmd)
is the reason you should have looked at `summarystats` before reading the table,
rather than after.
:::

```{julia}
# What did the data say about the overdispersion parameter?
φ_post = vec(chain_negbin[:φ])
println("φ posterior: median $(round(median(φ_post), digits = 2)), ",
        "95% interval [$(round(quantile(φ_post, 0.025), digits = 2)), ",
        "$(round(quantile(φ_post, 0.975), digits = 2))]")
```

**Honest question**: Why Negative Binomial?

- Mechanistic justification: Weak (no clear biological process)
- Empirical justification: Fits better than Poisson
- Convenience: Easy to compute, works with MCMC

**Is this really different from choosing a distance metric?**

# Interlude: Likelihood as Distance

## Likelihood as distance

The negative log-likelihood is actually a *distance function* between observed and predicted data:

$$\text{Distance} = -\log p(\text{obs} | \text{predicted})$$

We can see what distance each likelihood implies:

```{julia}
# Compare different observation models as distance functions
obs_val = 10.0
predicted_range = 1.0:0.5:20.0

# Poisson: -log P(obs | λ)
poisson_distance = [-logpdf(Poisson(λ), obs_val) for λ in predicted_range]

# Negative Binomial with different φ (convert to r,p parametrization)
# NegativeBinomial(r, p) where r=φ, p=φ/(φ+μ)
negbin_distance_phi5 = [-logpdf(NegativeBinomial(5.0, 5.0/(5.0+λ)), obs_val) for λ in predicted_range]
negbin_distance_phi20 = [-logpdf(NegativeBinomial(20.0, 20.0/(20.0+λ)), obs_val) for λ in predicted_range]

# Gaussian (for comparison)
gaussian_distance = [-logpdf(Normal(λ, 3.0), obs_val) for λ in predicted_range]

# Plot
plot(predicted_range, poisson_distance,
     label="Poisson", linewidth=2,
     xlabel="Predicted value", ylabel="-log(likelihood)",
     title="Different Likelihoods as Distance Functions (obs=10)",
     legend=:topright)
plot!(predicted_range, negbin_distance_phi5,
      label="NegBin(φ=5)", linewidth=2)
plot!(predicted_range, negbin_distance_phi20,
      label="NegBin(φ=20)", linewidth=2)
plot!(predicted_range, gaussian_distance,
      label="Gaussian(σ=3)", linewidth=2, linestyle=:dash)
```

This reveals that different likelihoods are just different ways of measuring distance:

- Poisson: Penalises deviations inversely proportional to predicted value
- Negative Binomial: Similar but allows more flexibility (overdispersion)
- Gaussian: Constant penalty regardless of scale

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning points"}

- Parametric likelihoods are pragmatic choices rather than mechanistic truths: we
  pick Poisson or negative binomial for convenience, not because they describe
  how reporting really works
- The Poisson assumption that variance equals the mean is testable, and
  surveillance data routinely breaks it
- A negative log-likelihood is a distance function, so choosing an observation
  model is choosing how to measure the gap between prediction and data
- An observation model that is too tight makes the posterior overconfident and
  lets a single unusual day dominate the fit

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: Which observation model for which system?"}
The choice is not abstract. For each of these surveillance systems, say which
observation model you would start with and what feature of the system drives the
answer.

1. A sentinel network of GP practices reporting influenza-like illness weekly,
   with stable participation and no weekend effect.
2. Notifications of a rare disease, where a single case triggers an investigation
   that often finds several more in the same household.
3. Deaths in a national registry, complete but reported with a delay that varies
   between one and three weeks.
4. A new pathogen where testing capacity tripled part-way through the outbreak.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
1. **Poisson is defensible.** Stable reporting, no obvious clustering, and cases
   arriving independently is roughly what Poisson assumes. Check the variance
   against the mean anyway rather than assuming.

2. **Negative binomial.** Case-finding around an index case produces exactly the
   clustering that breaks the independence assumption, and the visible symptom is
   variance far above the mean.

3. **Neither, on its own.** The problem here is not the spread but the *timing*:
   a case counted this week may belong to three weeks ago. No observation model
   fixes that. You need a delay distribution between the event and its report,
   which is a change to the model rather than to the likelihood family.

4. **Neither, again.** Tripling testing changes the proportion of infections you
   observe partway through, so a constant reporting fraction $\rho$ is wrong. You
   need $\rho$ to vary with time. Fitting a fixed $\rho$ here will make the model
   infer a change in transmission that never happened.

The general point: 1 and 2 are observation-model choices, 3 and 4 look like them
and are not. Asking "is this about how *much* noise, or about *what* the data
mean?" separates the two.
:::
